stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Each spring, collisions between warm Gulf air and cold continental air make the Great Plains one of the world's most active regions for severe weather. Towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains, ______ hail, lightning, and damaging winds within an hour of first appearing on radar.
choices: a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
the updrafts feeding a cumulonimbus cloud, which can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produces
a cumulonimbus cloud is fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, it often produces
explanation: Start by asking what is 'towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains.' It is the cloud, so the first noun after the comma has to be 'a cumulonimbus cloud.' Three choices pass that test, so finding the right subject is not enough. Next, check what follows it. The phrase 'fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour' is an interrupter. If you cross it out, you get 'a cumulonimbus cloud... often produces.' A singular subject takes the singular verb 'produces.' The sentence also needs exactly one main clause, and this choice gives it one. Only C meets all three conditions: the right subject, a verb that agrees with it, and a sound sentence boundary.

A.why: You found the right subject, then let the plural nouns in the interrupter ('updrafts,' 'kilometers') set the verb. The subject is still the singular 'cloud,' so 'produce' doesn't agree with it. It needs 'produces.'

B.why: You chose a noun closely related to the cloud instead of the cloud itself. Updrafts are rising air inside the cloud, and they don't 'tower' fifteen kilometers above the plains. Because 'the updrafts' comes first after the comma, the opening phrase is left dangling.

D.why: The opening noun is right, but this choice joins two independent clauses ('a cumulonimbus cloud is fed...' and 'it often produces...') with only a comma. That's a comma splice. Getting the subject right doesn't make up for a broken sentence boundary.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorists classify traditional stories by their recurring plot elements rather than by their country of origin, since a single plot often crosses many borders. Passed orally from one generation of storytellers to the next for centuries before anyone wrote it down, ______ today in more than forty regional variants.
choices: collectors in at least six countries have documented the ferryman tale, which survives
the ferryman tale, documented by collectors in at least six countries, survives
the ferryman tale, documented by collectors in at least six countries, survive
the ferryman tale was documented by collectors in at least six countries, it survives
explanation: Ask what was 'passed orally from one generation of storytellers to the next.' It was the tale, so 'the ferryman tale' has to be the first noun after the comma. Three choices start that way, so you still have to check the rest of the clause. Cross out the interrupter 'documented by collectors in at least six countries' and you are left with 'the ferryman tale... survives.' That is a singular subject with a singular verb, and the sentence has one main clause. Only B gets the subject, the agreement, and the sentence structure right.

A.why: You started with the people connected to the story instead of the story itself. The collectors weren't 'passed orally' between generations; the tale was. With 'collectors' first, the opening phrase describes the wrong noun, even though the rest of the choice reads smoothly.

C.why: You picked the right subject, then matched the verb to the plural nouns just before the blank ('collectors,' 'countries'). The subject is the singular 'tale,' so it needs 'survives,' not 'survive.'

D.why: This choice starts with the right noun but creates two independent clauses, 'the ferryman tale was documented...' and 'it survives...', joined only by a comma. That's a comma splice, so the sentence fails even though the modifier attaches correctly.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Linguists who study whistled languages have long asked how much of a spoken tongue a whistle can carry. On La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, herders still use Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish. Stripped of most vowel distinctions and reduced to rising and falling pitches, ______ across ravines more than two kilometers wide.
choices: the herders' messages, which listeners decode by context, carry
the herders, whose listeners decode the messages by context, send them
the messages of the herders, decoded by listeners from context, carries
listeners decode the herders' messages by context as they travel
explanation: The opening phrase describes something that has been stripped of vowel distinctions and reduced to pitches. Only the messages fit. In choice A, 'herders'' is a possessive that modifies the head noun 'messages', so the subject is 'messages'. That plural subject correctly takes 'carry', and the relative clause has its own finite verb, 'decode'.

B.why: You put the people who make the messages in the subject position. That says the herders themselves were stripped of vowels and reduced to pitches. This is the maker-for-the-thing trap.

C.why: You found the right subject, 'messages', but then matched the verb to the nearby singular noun 'context'. 'Messages' is plural and needs 'carry', not 'carries'.

D.why: You chose the people affected rather than the thing described. That makes the listeners the ones stripped of vowels and reduced to pitches.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a four-year trial in Iowa, agronomists compared fields planted with a winter cover of cereal rye against fields left bare between harvests. Rooted deeply enough to reach nitrate that would otherwise leach into groundwater, ______ the following spring.
choices: the rye, once tilled under, returning much of that nitrogen to the soil
the rye returned much of that nitrogen to the soil once it was tilled under
the agronomists found that the rye returned much of that nitrogen to the soil
the rye's nitrogen was returned to the soil once the plants were tilled under
explanation: Only a plant can be 'rooted deeply enough to reach nitrate', so the rye has to come right after the comma. Choice B starts with 'the rye' and gives it a finite main verb, 'returned', which makes the sentence complete.

A.why: You put the right noun first, but 'returning' is an -ing form and can't be a main verb. The sentence never gets a finite verb, so it's a fragment.

C.why: You let the researchers take the subject position. That says the agronomists were rooted in the soil. This is the trap of putting the people acting in the study in place of the plant.

D.why: 'Rye's' is only a possessive. The subject is 'nitrogen', a substance the rye took up, and nitrogen isn't rooted in anything. This is the trap of putting the object's property in place of the object.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Musicologists have traced many of Hildegard of Bingen's chants to a single twelfth-century manuscript, the Riesencodex. Copied by scribes working under her supervision and weighing roughly fifteen kilograms, ______ the most complete surviving record of her music.
choices: the Riesencodex, together with several smaller fragments, remain
Hildegard's chants survive in what is still
the Riesencodex, along with several smaller fragments, remains
the scribes produced what remains
explanation: Something that weighs about fifteen kilograms has to be a physical book, so the Riesencodex must come first. 'Along with several smaller fragments' is an interrupter, and it doesn't make the subject plural. The singular 'Riesencodex' takes 'remains'.

A.why: You chose the right subject, then let 'together with several smaller fragments' make it plural. Only 'and' makes a compound subject, so 'remain' should be 'remains'.

B.why: You chose the music the book contains rather than the book itself. Chants were copied, but they don't weigh fifteen kilograms.

D.why: You put the makers first. The scribes did the copying, so they couldn't also be the thing 'copied by scribes'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Bar-tailed godwits that breed in Alaska make one of the longest nonstop flights recorded for any bird. Having doubled their body weight in fat before departing and having flown for more than a week without landing, ______ New Zealand, some 11,000 kilometers away.
choices: the godwits' journey ends in
the godwits reach
the journey of the godwits ends in
the godwits, finally reaching
explanation: Only the birds put on fat and flew without landing, so 'the godwits' has to be the subject. Choice B also gives the sentence its finite main verb, 'reach'.

A.why: 'Godwits'' is only a possessive. The subject is 'journey', and a journey doesn't double its body weight. This is the trap of putting the thing that belongs to the birds in place of the birds.

C.why: 'The journey of the godwits' puts 'journey' first and pushes the birds into a prepositional phrase. The modifier now describes the journey.

D.why: You found the right subject, but 'reaching' is an -ing form and can't be a main verb. The sentence is left as a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The mimic octopus, first described from Indonesian waters in 1998, can impersonate a flatfish, a lionfish, or a venomous sea snake. Lacking any shell or spine and protected only by its skill at disguise, ______ that would ordinarily attack it.
choices: its imitations deter the predators
the predators are deterred by the octopus
the octopus deter the predators
the octopus deters the predators
explanation: The animal is the thing that lacks a shell and is protected by disguise, so 'the octopus' must come first. 'Octopus' is singular here, so it takes 'deters'.

A.why: You chose something the octopus produces rather than the octopus. Imitations don't lack a shell or spine. This is the trap of putting the creature's output in place of the creature.

B.why: The passive voice puts the predators first. That says the predators lack a shell and rely on disguise. This is the trap of putting those affected in place of the actor.

C.why: You chose the right subject, then probably let the plural 'predators' set the verb. 'The octopus' is singular and needs 'deters'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its main span was the longest of any suspension bridge in the world. Hung from four cables, each spun on site from more than 5,000 galvanized steel wires, ______ nearly 1,600 feet between its two granite towers.
choices: the deck, with its roadways and elevated promenade, stretches
the towers support a deck that stretches
the engineer Washington Roebling stretched the deck
the deck, with its roadways and elevated promenade, stretch
explanation: What hangs from the cables is the deck, so 'the deck' must follow the comma. The 'with...' phrase is an interrupter, and it doesn't make the subject plural, so singular 'deck' takes 'stretches'.

B.why: You chose a nearby structural part. The towers hold the cables up. They don't hang from them, so they can't be what the opening phrase describes.

C.why: You put the builder first. Roebling wasn't hung from four steel cables. This is the maker-for-the-thing trap.

D.why: You chose the right subject, then let the plural-sounding 'roadways and elevated promenade' set the verb. That phrase sits inside a 'with' interrupter, so the subject stays singular and needs 'stretches'.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 1569 the Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map on a projection that still bears his name. Drawn so that any line of constant compass bearing appears perfectly straight, ______ Greenland and Africa as roughly equal in size, though Africa is about fourteen times larger.
choices: Mercator's map, which shows
Mercator showed
the map's distortion shows
Mercator's map shows
explanation: A map is drawn, so the map must be the subject. 'Mercator's' is a possessive that modifies the head noun 'map'. Choice D also gives the sentence the finite main verb it needs, 'shows'.

A.why: You chose the right subject, but 'which shows' turns the verb into part of a relative clause. The subject 'map' never gets its own main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.why: You put the mapmaker first. Mercator wasn't drawn so that compass lines appear straight. This is the maker-for-the-thing trap.

C.why: 'Map's' is only a possessive. The subject is 'distortion', which is a property of the map, and the opening phrase describes the map. This is the trap of putting the property in place of the object.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In eighteenth-century Lyon, silk weavers depended on drawboys, who lifted bundles of warp threads by hand to form each row of a pattern. Woven at a pace of only a few centimeters a day and threaded with real gold and silver, ______ the most expensive textiles in Europe.
choices: Lyon's weavers produced
the brocades of Lyon ranking among
the brocades of Lyon ranked among
the brocades' gold and silver thread ranked among
explanation: The fabric is what gets woven and threaded with metal, so 'the brocades' must be the subject. Here, unlike the usual trap, the 'of' phrase follows the right noun and does no harm. 'Ranked' is the finite main verb the sentence needs.

A.why: You put the makers first. The weavers weren't woven or threaded with gold. This is the maker-for-the-thing trap.

B.why: You chose the right subject, but 'ranking' is an -ing form and can't be a main verb. The sentence is left as a fragment.

D.why: 'Brocades'' is only a possessive. The subject is 'thread', which is a material in the fabric. Thread isn't 'threaded with gold and silver'. This is the trap of putting the part in place of the whole.
